# Maghadeva Sutta (MN 83 (PTS MN ii 74))

**ID:** MN 83 (PTS MN ii 74)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Maghadeva Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** About King Maghadeva
**PTS:** MN ii 74
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Maghadeva Sutta* (MN 83, PTS MN ii 74; also known as the *Makhādeva Sutta*) is an extended mythic narrative in the *Majjhimanikāya* chronicling an ancient royal lineage and its eventual downfall. The narrative relates that King Maghadeva, upon observing the appearance of his first grey hair, abdicates his throne in favor of the crown prince and retires to his mango grove to live an ascetic life dedicated to the four "divine abodes" (*brahmavihāra*s: loving-kindness, compassion, altruistic joy, and equanimity) [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Dhammadinna 2013]. While this noble tradition of renunciation is sustained across generations of descendant monarchs, the Buddha explicitly points out the limitations of this past life of his as the Bodhisatta: king Maghadeva's practice leads merely to rebirth in the transient Brahmā world, whereas the Buddha's own teaching of the noble eightfold path leads directly to disenchantment, cessation, and nibbāna [Appleton, Buddha as Storyteller; Vetter 1988]. Kanai Lal Hazra notes that the composition of the discourse is traditionally placed later than the earliest verse strata such as the *Khaggavisāṇasutta* and the *Cullaniddesa* [Hazra 1994].

 While parallels such as MĀ 67 furnish elaborate descriptions of the seven treasures of a wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*), MN 83 omits this motif entirely [Anālayo 2017; Dhammadinna 2013]. DharmaNexus corroborates extensive alignments with MĀ 67, EĀ, the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D 1), and Up 2.050 (D 4094), while also highlighting dense Pali-internal text reuse with other mythic and doctrinal discourses, sharing extensive formulaic passages with DN 26 (*Cakkavatti Sutta*), DN 17 (*Mahāsudassana Sutta*), and DN 19 (*Mahāgovinda Sutta*) [DharmaNexus].
